edition.locus: Divine Institutes 6.2 (lumina inania / mens lumen / uictus inmaculata)

source_text: Mactant igitur opimas ac pingues hostias deo quasi esurienti, profundunt uina tamquam sitienti, accendunt lumina uelut in tenebris agenti. quodsi suspicari aut percipere animo possint quae sint bona illa caelestia, quorum magnitudinem terreno adhuc corpore obuoluti sensu capere non possumus, iam se cum his officiis inanibus stultissimos esse cognoscant, uel si caeleste lumen quod dicimus solem contemplari nelint, iam sentiant quam non indigeat lucernis eorum deus, qui ipse in usum hominis tam claram, tam candidam lucem dedit. et tamen cum in tam paruo circulo, qui propter longinquitatem non amplius quam humani capitis uidetur habere mensuram, tantum sit fulgoris, ut eum mortalium luminum acies non queat contueri et si paulisper intenderis, hebetatos oculos caligo ac tenebrae consequantur, quid tandem luminis, quid claritatis aput ipsum deum, penes quem nulla nox est, esse arbitremur? qui hanc ipsam lucem sic moderatus est, ut neque nimio fulgore neque calore uehementi noceret animantibus tantumque istarum rerum dedit ei, quantum aut mortalia corpora pati possent aut frugum maturitas postularet. num igitur mentis suae compos putandus est qui auctori et datori luminis candelarum aut cerarum lumen offert pro munere? aliut uero ille a nobis exigit lumen et quidem non fumidum, sed, ut ait poeta, liquidum atque clarum, mentis scilicet, propter quod a poetis Ϟω̃τες nuncupamur: quod exhibere non potest nisi qui deum agnouerit. illorum autem dii quia terreni sunt, egent luminibus, ne in tenebris sint: quorum cultores quia caeleste nihil sapiunt, etiam religiones quibus deseruiunt ad terram reuocant: in ea enim lumine opus est, quia ratio eius et natura tenebrosa est. itaque diis non caelestem sensum, sed humanum potius adtribuunt ideoque illis necessaria et grata credunt esse quae nobis, quibus aut esurientibus opus est cibo aut sitientibus potu aut ueste algentibus aut cum sol decesserit lumine, ut uidere possimus. nullis igitur ex rebus tam probari et intellegi potest deos istos, cum aliquando uixerint, mortuos esse quam ex ipso ritu, qui est totus e terra. quid enim caelestis in se boni potest habere pecudum sanguis effusus, quo aras inquinant? nisi forte deos existimant eo uesci quod homines aspernantur attingere. et quisquis illis hanc saginam praestiterit, quamuis ille grassator adulter ueneficus parricida sit, beatus ac felix erit, hunc diligunt, hunc tuentur, huic omnia quae optauerit praestant. merito ergo Persius huiusmodi superstitiones suo more deridet: qua tu inquit mercede deorum emeris auriculas? pulmone et lactibus unctis ? sentiebat uidelicet non carne opus esse ad placaudam caelestem maiestatem, sed mente sancta et iusto animo et pectore, ut ipse ait, quod naturali sit honestate generosum. haec est religio caelestis, non quae constat ei rebus corruptis, sed quae uirtutibus animi qui oritur e caelo, hic uerus est cultus, in quo mens colentis se ipsam deo inmaculatam uictimam sistit. id autem ipsum quomodo consequendum, quomodo praestandum sit, docebit huius libri disputatio. nihil enim tam praeclarum hominique conueniens potest esse quam erudire homines ad iustitiam. aput Ciceronem Catulus in Hortensio philosophiam rebus omnibus praeferens malle se dicit uel unum paruum de officio libellum quam longam orationem pro seditioso homine Cornelio. quae sententia non utique Catuli, qui illut fortasse non dixit, sed Ciceronis est putanda, qui scripsit, credo ut libros quos de officiis erat scripturus commendaret: in quibus ipsis nihil esse testatur in omni philosophia melius et fructuosius quam praecepta uitae dare. quodsi hoc illi faciunt quibus non est ueritas cognita, quanto magis nos facere debemus qui a deo eruditi et inluminati possumus uera praecipere! nec tamen sic docebimus ut quasi prima uirtutis elementa tradamus, quod est infinitum, sed tamquam docendum susceperimus eum qui aput illos iam perfectus esse uideatur. manentibus enim praeceptis eorum quae solent ad probitatem recte dare, ignota illis superstruemus ad perficiendam consummandamque iustitiam, quam non tenent. ea uero quae possunt cum illis esse communia praetermittam, ne quid ab iis uidear mutuari quorum errores coarguere atque aperire decreuerim.
pass_a_gloss: They fatten God as if he hungered, pour wine as if he thirsted, light lamps as if he sat in the dark — empty offices if they knew heavenly goods or even the sun he gave. He asks not smoky candlelight but clear light of the mind, which only the one who has known God can offer. True religion is not corrupt goods but virtues of the soul born from heaven: true worship is the worshiper's mind setting itself before God as an unblemished victim.
pass_b_english: They therefore sacrifice rich and fat victims to God as if to one hungry, pour out wines as if to one thirsty, kindle lights as if to one living in darkness. But if they could suspect or perceive in mind what those heavenly goods are, whose greatness we, still wrapped in an earthly body, cannot grasp by sense, they would already know themselves most foolish with these empty offices; or if they would gaze on the heavenly light which we call the sun, they would already feel how little God needs their lamps, who himself gave for human use so bright, so white a light. And yet when in so small a circle, which because of distance seems to have measure no more than a human head, there is so much brilliance that the edge of mortal eyes cannot look on it and if you aim a little, dullness and darkness follow the weakened eyes, what light finally, what brightness should we think is with God himself, with whom there is no night? Who moderated this very light so that it would not harm living things by too much brilliance or violent heat and gave it only so much of those things as either mortal bodies could bear or the ripening of crops required. Is he then to be thought master of his mind who offers to the author and giver of light the light of candles or wax as a gift? But that one demands from us another light and indeed not smoky, but, as the poet says, liquid and clear — namely of the mind — for which we are called φῶτες by the poets: which none can show except who has recognized God.

But their gods, because they are earthly, need lights lest they be in darkness: whose worshipers, because they taste nothing heavenly, also call back to earth the religions they serve: for in it there is need of light, because its reason and nature is dark. And so they attribute to the gods not heavenly sense but rather human and therefore believe necessary and pleasing to them what is to us, who when hungry need food or when thirsty drink or when cold clothing or when the sun has withdrawn light, that we may see. By no things therefore can it be so proved and understood that those gods, since they once lived, are dead as by the rite itself, which is wholly from earth. For what heavenly good can poured blood of cattle have in itself, with which they stain the altars? Unless perhaps they think the gods feed on that which humans refuse to touch. And whoever has provided them this stuffing, though he be a robber, adulterer, poisoner, parricide, will be blessed and happy; him they love, him they protect, to him they grant all he has wished. Deservedly therefore Persius mocks superstitions of this sort in his manner: 'By what wage,' he says, 'will you buy the gods' ears? With lung and greased guts?' He sensed clearly that flesh is not needed to placate heavenly majesty, but a holy mind and a just spirit and a breast, as he himself says, that is noble with natural honesty.

This is heavenly religion, not which consists of corrupt things, but which consists of virtues of the soul which rises from heaven; this is true worship, in which the worshiper's mind sets itself before God as an unblemished victim. But how that itself is to be attained, how it is to be rendered, this book's dispute will teach. For nothing can be so excellent and fitting for a human than to train humans to justice. In Cicero, Catulus in the Hortensius, preferring philosophy to all things, says he would rather have even one small booklet on duty than a long speech for the seditious man Cornelius. Which sentence is not certainly Catulus's, who perhaps did not say that, but is to be thought Cicero's, who wrote it, I believe that he might commend the books he was going to write on duties: in which themselves he testifies that there is nothing in all philosophy better and more fruitful than to give precepts of life. And if those do this who have not known the truth, how much more ought we to do it who, taught and illuminated by God, can give true precepts! And yet we will not teach so as to hand over as it were the first elements of virtue, which is endless, but as if we have undertaken to teach him who among them already seems perfect. For with their precepts remaining which they are accustomed to give rightly toward honesty, we will build on what is unknown to them to perfect and complete justice, which they do not hold. But those things that can be common with them I will pass by, lest I seem to borrow anything from those whose errors I have decided to convict and open.

lemmas.gloss: God asks mind's clear light, not smoky lamps
holy mind placates majesty, not fat flesh
true worship: mind as unblemished victim

rejected: candles and fat victims feed God's need
choices.why: The giver of the sun wants the mind's clear light, not smoky lamps.

choices.why: Heavenly majesty is placated by a holy mind, not sacrificial stuffing.

rejected: true cult is only correct outdoor rite
